title: A Song for Nobody Else
subtitle: Stars Between the Strings · Chapter 28 of 40
content:
The page fell out of Greg's song notebook when I moved it off the porch chair.

I hadn't gone looking. A gust of wind lifted the cover, the paper slipped free, and there was Rose's name in handwriting I knew belonged to a younger Greg.

For a moment I couldn't move.

It was a list of unfinished chords and a line about somebody laughing at the sea. Nothing cruel. Nothing secret in any meaningful sense. And still I felt the uncomfortable flash of jealousy that arrived before I could decide what kind of person I wanted to be.

Greg came through the door with two drinks.

"Hey, you found the notebook."

I held up the loose page.

"It fell out."

He saw the name and stopped.

"Oh."

"I didn't read the whole thing."

"You're allowed to read it."

"Are you sure?"

He set the drinks down.

"Actually, can I think about that?"

I nodded and offered the page back. He took it gently, then sat on the step beside the chair.

For a while we watched the light move over the water.

"I wrote that after a show," he said at last. "I wasn't very good at finishing songs back then. I thought if I got the ending right, I'd understand what happened."

"You don't owe me an explanation."

"I know. I want to tell you why I kept it."

I sat beside him.

"Okay."

"Because it was part of my life. Because Steven's mom mattered. Because I did some good things and some stupid things, and pretending I don't remember them wouldn't make me a better partner now."

I looked down at my hands.

"That makes sense."

He studied me.

"Are you upset?"

"A little."

"At me?"

"Not exactly. I think I'm jealous of the certainty a piece of paper seems to have. It was there before me. It has her name on it. My brain wants to act like there's only room for one person in a notebook."

Greg blinked, then laughed softly.

"Believe me, that notebook has room for way too much."

I smiled despite myself.

He looked out at the sea again.

"Sometimes I don't know what to do when somebody I love feels like they have to compete with a memory. I don't want to erase Rose. I don't want to hurt you, either."

"I don't want you to erase her."

"Good."

"But I need to know you're not comparing every version of us to a song you never finished."

He considered the question seriously.

"No," he said. "I'm not. You're not a replacement, Jasper. You make me laugh in different places. You argue with me about the car wash. You tell me when I accidentally volunteer for six jobs. You show up with stories about a square full of lanterns and people who argue over sidewalks."

"Those people do argue."

"I know. I like hearing about them."

He held the page between two fingers.

"Can I keep this without making it something you have to live up to?"

"Yes."

"Then I'd like to."

I took a breath.

We had talked about my being ethically non-monogamous and preferring polyamory before we started dating seriously. I'd asked him to accept that the other people in my life would not disappear. It was strange to discover how hard it could still feel when I met the shape of someone who would never be here to explain herself.

"I guess I have to practice the same generosity," I said.

"You don't have to feel perfect about it."

"Thank goodness."

He smiled and closed the notebook.

"Want to hear a new piece instead?"

"Only if you actually want to play it."

He picked up the guitar.

It was a small, bright melody that ended too soon. I liked it immediately.

"Why'd you stop?"

"That's all I've got."

"Play it again."

He did.

The third time, I hummed a low note beneath the ending. He paused.

"That's not where I thought it was going."

"Good not where or bad not where?"

"Interesting."

He made a mark in the margin.

We were creating something without covering the old page or pretending it meant less than it did. Greg played the melody once more, then put the guitar aside.

"Should we go for a walk?" he asked.

"Yes."

Before we left, he asked whether I wanted him to put the page away where I wouldn't see it again.

"No," I said. "I want you to decide where it belongs. I just want to know I can tell you when something catches me off guard."

He looked relieved.

"That's a deal."

He returned it to the notebook without asking me to watch, then found the small bag of trash we'd forgotten to take out after the last storm.

"I was going to carry this down to the bins," he said. "Want to come?"

"I thought we were going for a romantic walk."

"We can be very romantic while throwing away a torn paper cup."

I laughed.

The path was nearly empty. I carried the lighter bag while Greg carried the one with the broken plastic fragments. At the bins, we sorted them according to the posted rules. He checked the notice twice because he wasn't sure where the foil wrappers went.

It would have been easier for him to make a joke and leave the bag for someone else to handle. Instead he asked a volunteer and did it properly.

When we returned to the boardwalk, Greg brushed sand from his hands.

"Maybe that's what I want from us," he said. "Not everything neatly resolved. Just being able to ask the weird question without having to run."

I reached for his hand.

"I can try that."

He squeezed once.

"Me too."

We took the shore path. A small group of children was practicing a beach cleanup by the lower steps, sorting plastic from driftwood under the supervision of a volunteer. Greg stopped to thank them. He didn't make himself the leader; he asked whether they needed another pair of hands. They had enough.

"Imagine that," he said. "A problem being handled without me."

"A miracle."

He laughed.

At the far bench, I asked whether I could kiss him. He said yes, and I did, warm and a little awkward when the wind blew his hair across both our faces.

We walked home holding hands.

That evening he asked if I wanted to spend the night. I did. We set the notebook safely on its shelf before closing the door.

The next morning the page was still inside.

Before breakfast, Steven stopped by to return a borrowed cable.

Greg told him the new melody was coming along. Steven asked if he could listen when it was finished, and Greg said yes.

"What kind of song?" Steven asked.

"Still figuring that out."

He didn't mention Rose's page. The old memory belonged to him, and Steven didn't need to become an audience for my jealousy or for Greg's uncertainty.

After Steven left, I asked Greg whether he wanted the new song to have a title.

"Maybe later. I'm not even sure the bridge is right."

"Then leave it unfinished for now."

He looked at me.

"You're good at letting things stay complicated."

"I'm practicing."

He laughed and found the notebook where he'd left it.

I took my coffee to the porch. There were places I loved beyond this beach, and people there whose histories I could never entirely know either. I wouldn't ask their pasts to shrink around me just so the present could be easier.

Greg joined me with his guitar. He played the unfinished chord once, then waited for me to hum the note we'd discovered together.

I did.

It still sounded unusual. We kept it.

Greg showed me where he'd placed it. Not hidden, not displayed as a test. Just part of the book.

I didn't need to be first in every chapter of his life.

I needed the part we were writing together to be real.
